1(c)

Income was approximated using interval midpoints because the original survey data recorded household income only in categories rather than as exact continuous values. For the open-ended category of \$100,000 or more, \$125,000 was assigned as a representative value. The broad categories “under \$20,000” and “\$20,000 or more,” as well as refused, unknown, and missing responses, were treated as missing in the numeric income variable. Income was expressed in units of \$10,000. Observations with missing model variables were excluded from the corresponding models.

```{r}
# Prepare tympanometric width outcomes.
nhanes$width_right <- as.numeric(nhanes$AUXTWIDR)
nhanes$width_left <- as.numeric(nhanes$AUXTWIDL)

nhanes$width_right[
  nhanes$width_right %in% c(555, 777, 888)
] <- NA

nhanes$width_left[
  nhanes$width_left %in% c(555, 777, 888)
] <- NA
nhanes$gender <- relevel(
  nhanes$gender,
  ref = "Male"
)

nhanes$children_num <- as.numeric(nhanes$DMDHHSZA)

income_midpoints <- c(
  "1" = 2500,
  "2" = 7500,
  "3" = 12500,
  "4" = 17500,
  "5" = 22500,
  "6" = 30000,
  "7" = 40000,
  "8" = 50000,
  "9" = 60000,
  "10" = 70000,
  "14" = 87500,
  "15" = 125000
)

nhanes$income_10k <- unname(
  income_midpoints[
    as.character(nhanes$INDHHIN2)
  ]
) / 10000

model_1R <- glm(
  width_right ~ gender,
  data = nhanes,
  family = poisson(link = "log"),
  na.action = na.omit
)

model_2R <- glm(
  width_right ~ gender + citizenship + children_num + income_10k,
  data = nhanes,
  family = poisson(link = "log"),
  na.action = na.omit
)

model_1L <- glm(
  width_left ~ gender,
  data = nhanes,
  family = poisson(link = "log"),
  na.action = na.omit
)

model_2L <- glm(
  width_left ~ gender + citizenship + children_num + income_10k,
  data = nhanes,
  family = poisson(link = "log"),
  na.action = na.omit
)

#'
#' @param model A fitted Poisson glm object.
#' @param model_name A character label identifying the model.
#' @return A data frame of IRRs, Wald confidence intervals, and p-values.
extract_irr <- function(model, model_name) {
  coefficient_table <- coef(summary(model))

  estimates <- coefficient_table[, "Estimate"]
  standard_errors <- coefficient_table[, "Std. Error"]
  critical_value <- qnorm(0.975)

  data.frame(
    Model = model_name,
    Term = rownames(coefficient_table),
    IRR = exp(estimates),
    CI_lower = exp(estimates - critical_value * standard_errors),
    CI_upper = exp(estimates + critical_value * standard_errors),
    p_value = coefficient_table[, "Pr(>|z|)"],
    row.names = NULL
  )
}

irr_table <- rbind(
  extract_irr(model_1R, "1R"),
  extract_irr(model_2R, "2R"),
  extract_irr(model_1L, "1L"),
  extract_irr(model_2L, "2L")
)

term_labels <- c(
  "(Intercept)" = "Intercept: exp(beta0)",
  "genderFemale" = "Female vs Male",
  "citizenshipNot a US citizen" = "Non-US citizen vs US citizen",
  "children_num" = "Children: per additional child",
  "income_10k" = "Income: per $10,000 increase"
)

irr_table$Term <- unname(
  term_labels[irr_table$Term]
)

irr_display <- irr_table

irr_display$p_value <- format.pval(
  irr_display$p_value,
  digits = 3,
  eps = 0.001
)

knitr::kable(
  irr_display,
  digits = 3,
  col.names = c(
    "Model", "Coefficient", "IRR",
    "95% CI lower", "95% CI upper", "p-value"
  ),
  caption = "Exponentiated coefficients from Poisson regression models"
)

#' Extract model fit statistics
#'
#' @param model A fitted Poisson glm object.
#' @param model_name A character label identifying the model.
#' @return A data frame containing sample size, McFadden R-squared, and AIC.
extract_fit <- function(model, model_name) {
  model_data <- model.frame(model)

  null_model <- glm(
    update(formula(model), . ~ 1),
    data = model_data,
    family = poisson(link = "log")
  )

  pseudo_r2 <- 1 -
    as.numeric(logLik(model)) /
    as.numeric(logLik(null_model))

  data.frame(
    Model = model_name,
    N = nobs(model),
    McFadden_R2 = pseudo_r2,
    AIC = AIC(model)
  )
}

fit_table <- rbind(
  extract_fit(model_1R, "1R"),
  extract_fit(model_2R, "2R"),
  extract_fit(model_1L, "1L"),
  extract_fit(model_2L, "2L")
)

knitr::kable(
  fit_table,
  digits = c(0, 0, 4, 2),
  col.names = c("Model", "Sample size", "McFadden pseudo-R²", "AIC"),
  caption = "Poisson model fit statistics"
)

```

In model 2L, the female-to-male IRR was 1.0189 (95% CI: 1.0118–1.0262; Wald $z=5.215$, $p=1.84\times10^{-7}$). After adjustment for citizenship, number of children, and household income, females had approximately 1.9% greater predicted mean left-ear tympanometric width than males.

The adjusted predicted means were 84.18 for males and 85.77 for females. The female-minus-male difference was 1.595 (95% CI: 0.996–2.194; $z=5.218$, $p<0.001$). Thus, we reject equality of the adjusted predicted means.

```{r}
#' Summarize customers by store using R
#'
#' @param con An open DBI database connection.
#' @return A data frame of customer counts and active percentages by store.
customers_r <- function(con) {
  stores <- dbGetQuery(
    con,
    "SELECT store_id FROM store"
  )

  customers <- dbGetQuery(
    con,
    "SELECT customer_id, store_id, active FROM customer"
  )

  customers$active_count <- as.integer(customers$active == 1)

  counts <- aggregate(
    cbind(customer_id, active_count) ~ store_id,
    data = customers,
    FUN = length
  )

  active_counts <- aggregate(
    active_count ~ store_id,
    data = customers,
    FUN = sum
  )

  result <- merge(
    stores,
    counts[c("store_id", "customer_id")],
    by = "store_id",
    all.x = TRUE
  )

  names(result)[2] <- "customer_count"

  result <- merge(
    result,
    active_counts,
    by = "store_id",
    all.x = TRUE
  )

  result$customer_count[is.na(result$customer_count)] <- 0
  result$active_count[is.na(result$active_count)] <- 0

  result$active_percentage <- ifelse(
    result$customer_count > 0,
    100 * result$active_count / result$customer_count,
    NA_real_
  )

  result <- result[
    order(result$store_id),
    c("store_id", "customer_count", "active_percentage")
  ]

  rownames(result) <- NULL
  result
}

result_a_r <- customers_r(con)

print(
  knitr::kable(
    result_a_r,
    digits = 2,
    col.names = c("Store ID", "Customers", "Active customers (%)"),
    caption = "Customer counts and active percentages by store"
  )
)
```

use Sql:

```{r}
sql_a <- "
SELECT
  s.store_id,
  COUNT(c.customer_id) AS customer_count,
  100.0 * SUM(
    CASE WHEN c.active = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END
  ) / NULLIF(COUNT(c.customer_id), 0) AS active_percentage
FROM store AS s
LEFT JOIN customer AS c
  ON s.store_id = c.store_id
GROUP BY s.store_id
ORDER BY s.store_id
"

result_a_sql <- dbGetQuery(con, sql_a)
```

test and compare:

```{r}
all.equal(
  result_a_r,
  result_a_sql,
  check.attributes = FALSE
)

benchmark_a <- microbenchmark(
  R_operations = customers_r(con),
  SQL_query = dbGetQuery(con, sql_a),
  times = 100L
)

kable(
  summary(benchmark_a, unit = "ms"),
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Runtime comparison for part (a), in milliseconds"
)
```

Both approaches produced the same results. Across 100 runs per approach, the median runtime was 4.181 ms for the R approach and 0.779 ms for the SQL approach. Thus, the SQL approach was approximately 5.37 times as fast based on median runtime.

```{r}
#' Find staff names and countries using R joins
#'
#' @param con An open DBI database connection.
#' @return A data frame containing staff IDs, names, and countries.
staff_r <- function(con) {
  staff <- dbGetQuery(
    con,
    "SELECT staff_id, first_name, last_name, address_id FROM staff"
  )

  addresses <- dbGetQuery(
    con,
    "SELECT address_id, city_id FROM address"
  )

  cities <- dbGetQuery(
    con,
    "SELECT city_id, country_id FROM city"
  )

  countries <- dbGetQuery(
    con,
    "SELECT country_id, country FROM country"
  )

  result <- merge(staff, addresses, by = "address_id")
  result <- merge(result, cities, by = "city_id")
  result <- merge(result, countries, by = "country_id")

  result$name <- paste(result$first_name, result$last_name)

  result <- result[
    order(result$staff_id),
    c("staff_id", "name", "country")
  ]

  rownames(result) <- NULL
  result
}

result_b_r <- staff_r(con)

kable(
  result_b_r,
  col.names = c("Staff ID", "Name", "Country"),
  caption = "Staff names and countries"
)
```

use Sql:

```{r}
sql_b <- "
SELECT
  s.staff_id,
  s.first_name || ' ' || s.last_name AS name,
  co.country
FROM staff AS s
JOIN address AS a
  ON s.address_id = a.address_id
JOIN city AS ci
  ON a.city_id = ci.city_id
JOIN country AS co
  ON ci.country_id = co.country_id
ORDER BY s.staff_id
"

result_b_sql <- dbGetQuery(con, sql_b)
```

check and compare:

```{r}
all.equal(

)

kable(
  summary(benchmark_b, unit = "ms"),
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Runtime comparison for part (b), in milliseconds"
)
```

Both approaches produced the same results. Across 100 runs per approach, the median runtime was 4.528 ms for the R approach and 0.721 ms for the SQL approach. Thus, the SQL approach was approximately 6.28 times as fast based on median runtime.

use R:

```{r}
#' Find films with the highest payment total for a single rental
#'
#' @param con An open DBI database connection.
#' @return A data frame containing film IDs, titles, and maximum rental value.
films_r <- function(con) {
  payments <- dbGetQuery(
    con,
    "SELECT rental_id, amount
     FROM payment
     WHERE rental_id IS NOT NULL"
  )

  rentals <- dbGetQuery(
    con,
    "SELECT rental_id, inventory_id FROM rental"
  )

  inventory <- dbGetQuery(
    con,
    "SELECT inventory_id, film_id FROM inventory"
  )

  films <- dbGetQuery(
    con,
    "SELECT film_id, title FROM film"
  )

  rental_values <- aggregate(
    amount ~ rental_id,
    data = payments,
    FUN = sum
  )

  highest_value <- max(rental_values$amount)

  highest_rentals <- rental_values[
    rental_values$amount == highest_value,
    ,
    drop = FALSE
  ]

  result <- merge(highest_rentals, rentals, by = "rental_id")
  result <- merge(result, inventory, by = "inventory_id")
  result <- merge(result, films, by = "film_id")

  result <- unique(result[c("film_id", "title", "amount")])

  names(result)[3] <- "rental_value"

  result <- result[order(result$film_id), ]
  rownames(result) <- NULL
  result
}

result_c_r <- films_r(con)

kable(
  result_c_r,
  digits = 2,
  col.names = c("Film ID", "Title", "Rental value (USD)"),
  caption = "Films with the highest single-rental value"
)
```

use Sql:

```{r}
sql_c <- "
WITH rental_values AS (
  SELECT
    rental_id,
    SUM(amount) AS rental_value
  FROM payment
  WHERE rental_id IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY rental_id
)
SELECT DISTINCT
  f.film_id,
  f.title,
  rv.rental_value
FROM rental_values AS rv
JOIN rental AS r
  ON rv.rental_id = r.rental_id
JOIN inventory AS i
  ON r.inventory_id = i.inventory_id
JOIN film AS f
  ON i.film_id = f.film_id
WHERE rv.rental_value = (
  SELECT MAX(rental_value)
  FROM rental_values
)
ORDER BY f.film_id
"

result_c_sql <- dbGetQuery(con, sql_c)
```

check and compare:

```{r}
all.equal(
  result_c_r,
  result_c_sql,
  check.attributes = FALSE
)

  times = 100L
)

kable(
  summary(benchmark_c, unit = "ms"),
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Runtime comparison for part (c), in milliseconds"
)
```

Both approaches produced the same results. Across 100 runs per approach, the median runtime was 198.486 ms for the R approach and 10.804 ms for the SQL approach. Thus, the SQL approach was approximately 18.37 times as fast based on median runtime.

```{r}
#' Format ten-digit phone numbers in a 4-3-3 pattern
#'
#' @param x A character vector of phone numbers.
#' @return A character vector formatted as XXXX-XXX-XXX.
format_phone <- function(x) {
  digits <- gsub("[^0-9]", "", x)

  invalid <- !is.na(digits) & nchar(digits) != 10

  if (any(invalid)) {
    stop("Some phone numbers do not contain exactly 10 digits.")
  }

  sub(
    "^([0-9]{4})([0-9]{3})([0-9]{3})$",
    "\\1-\\2-\\3",
    digits
  )
}

australia$phone1_cell <- format_phone(australia$phone1)
australia$phone2_cell <- format_phone(australia$phone2)

result_d <- head(
  australia[c("phone1_cell", "phone2_cell")],
  10
)

knitr::kable(
  result_d,
  col.names = c("Phone 1", "Phone 2"),
  caption = "First ten phone numbers in 4-3-3 format"
)
```

3(f)

```{r}
leading_digit <- as.integer(
  substr(
    as.character(positive_apartments),
    start = 1,
    stop = 1
  )
)

observed_counts <- table(
  factor(leading_digit, levels = 1:9)
)

benford_prob <- log10(1 + 1 / (1:9))

result_f <- data.frame(
  Leading_digit = 1:9,
  Observed_count = as.integer(observed_counts),
  Observed_proportion = as.integer(observed_counts) /
    sum(observed_counts),
  Benford_proportion = benford_prob
)

knitr::kable(
  result_f,
  digits = 4,
  caption = "Observed leading digits compared with Benford's law"
)

comparison <- rbind(
  Observed = result_f$Observed_proportion,
  Benford = result_f$Benford_proportion
)

barplot(
  comparison,
  beside = TRUE,
  names.arg = 1:9,
  col = c("steelblue", "orange"),
  legend.text = rownames(comparison),
  args.legend = list(x = "topright", bty = "n"),
  main = "Leading digits of apartment numbers",
  xlab = "Leading digit",
  ylab = "Proportion",
  ylim = c(0, max(comparison) * 1.25)
)

benford_test <- chisq.test(
  x = as.integer(observed_counts),
  p = benford_prob
)

benford_test
```

The leading digits of the 130 positive apartment numbers do not appear to follow Benford’s law. For example, only 9.23% begin with 1, compared with the expected 30.10%, while 14.62% begin with 9, compared with the expected 4.58%. A chi-squared goodness-of-fit test rejects the Benford distribution, $chi^2(8)=62.268$, $p=1.67\times10^{-10}$.

These numbers would not pass a Benford-based screening. However, apartment numbers are assigned identifiers and need not follow Benford’s law even when genuine. Therefore, this result alone cannot establish that the data are fabricated.
